narrator.instruct: Gripping, energetic storyteller telling a true, funny computer history story with wonder, brisk, excited and punchy, never calm.

operator.instruct: A young computer operator in 1947 writing a logbook entry out loud, deadpan and proud of his own joke, crisp and quick.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The most famous computer bug in history was an actual bug, trapped inside a giant machine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Harvard, September ninth, nineteen forty-seven. The Mark II computer was being tested. It was a room full of relays, tiny switches that a magnet clicks shut.
lines.say: Harvard, September ninth, nineteen forty-seven. The Mark Two computer was being tested. It was a room full of relays, tiny switches that a magnet clicks shut.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But that afternoon, right in the middle of a test, the operators traced an error.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They searched the whole machine, panel by panel, relay by relay.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: At fifteen forty-five, in Panel F, Relay number seventy, they found it: a moth, trapped between the contact points.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They pulled it out, taped it into the logbook, and wrote one line.

lines.speaker: operator
lines.text: First actual case of bug being found.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You see, a relay works only when its two contacts touch. The magnet pulls them together, and the current flows on. With a moth's body in the way, they could not close.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the word bug was already old. Thomas Edison wrote about bugs back in eighteen seventy-eight.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The joke stuck, and Grace Hopper, who worked on the machine, told the story again and again.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So today the page, moth and all, is kept at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the first actual bug is still taped right there on that page.
